title: "Congrats! Now Go Talk to an Audience that Doesn't Want to Listen to You."
author: Daniel Golazeski
summary: Daniel Golazeski, writing at Teach Students, Not Classes, reproduces the speech he gave as his district's Teacher of the Year, delivered to a restless auditorium of exhausted colleagues on the first in-service day of a new school year. He opens with a self-deprecating story about his grandfather, a thirty-five-year math teacher, before turning to the speech's real argument: that a teacher's offhand words carry more lasting weight with students than any of the formal accountability apparatus -- SGOs, SGPs, walk-throughs, observations -- that structures a teacher's year. His evidence is a personal memory of a former history teacher, Mr. Romano, who stopped him in a hallway three years after having taught him to compliment a newspaper photo of his pole-vaulting success -- a moment Golazeski says the teacher likely forgot but he never has. The speech closes by extending the same claim forward to his colleagues: they too will say something this year that a student remembers for the rest of their life, so the charge is simply to give students their best.
points: Golazeski's central claim is that a teacher's brief, offhand words to a student outweigh, in lasting impact, the entire formal accountability apparatus of SGOs, walk-throughs, and observations that structures a teacher's year.

His evidence is autobiographical: a former history teacher who stopped him in a hallway three years after having taught him, to compliment a newspaper photo, in a moment Golazeski believes the teacher has since forgotten but that Golazeski says he will remember for the rest of his life.

He extends the argument to the same colleagues he was addressing, noting that educators in that very room had encouraged him as a struggling student teacher a decade earlier -- proof, in his framing, that the effect he's describing is not hypothetical.

The speech's closing charge to teachers beginning a new year is explicit: this year, each of them will say something a student remembers for the rest of their life, so the job is simply to give students their best.
quotes: Every year we face SGO's, SGP's, walk-throughs, formal observations, action plans, and mountains of other paperwork, but students value our words much more than any of that stuff. I know this, because I experienced it when I was a student.
In high school, like many students, I lacked any sort of true self-confidence, I was constantly struggling to handle my emotions in a mature manner, and my social skills left a lot to be desired.

Mr. Romano had taught me three years earlier when I was a freshman, and I was sure he had forgotten me. In my mind, I was so insignificant that I was unworthy of note in his memory. But with a very brief interaction, Mr. Romano showed me I was wrong.
It's very possible Mr. Romano has completely forgotten our conversation, but I will remember it for the rest of my life.

Many educators in this room shared encouraging words with me when I was a struggling student teacher here ten years ago. Maybe you have forgotten about them, but I haven't. Your words make a difference. Always remember that.

This year you will be lucky enough to share in a student's joy, and a student will be lucky that they have someone like you to share in their sorrow. This year you will say something that a student will remember for the rest of their life.
